Improving robots’ fine motor skills

Hausman was impressed that RT-2 was able to move a Coke can to Taylor Swift. But later in the same interview, he described it as “totally unimpressive” and a “pretty pathetic demonstration of what robots could do.” That sounds like a contradiction, but you can see what he meant if you watch the video:

You can view all the RT-2 videos on this page. You’ll see that this was far from the only time the robot was hilariously clumsy. Another trial asked a robot to place a strawberry in a bowl. The gripper grabbed the strawberry and then lurched back and forth indecisively for several seconds before finally — just barely — heaving it into the correct container.

A key challenge was action frequency. Ideally, a robot should receive fresh instructions about 50 times per second, but RT-2 couldn’t generate actions that quickly. The smallest version of RT-2, with 5 billion parameters, generated about five actions per second. Larger versions were even slower. This made the robot’s motions jerky and erratic.

To speed things up, PI models engage in “action chunking”: they generate as many as 50 sequential actions using a technique called flow matching. Flow matching is a cousin of the diffusion techniques used in many generative image models. Whereas LLMs generate one token at a time, flow-matching models can generate all 50 actions in parallel.2 This means the robot is never waiting around for the model to send it the next instruction.

Flow matching has another advantage too: it isn’t constrained to output discrete values. Earlier, I said that RT-2 would output actions like “1 128 91 241 5 101 127 217,” where 128 (for example) was the x coordinate the robot’s gripper should move to next. These numbers are all integers because LLMs output discrete tokens.3

In contrast, flow matching enables PI models to natively generate decimal values like 127.5 or 127.351; they aren’t forced to choose between integers like 127 or 128. This allows PI’s models to control robots more smoothly and precisely.

This approach has rapidly become an industry standard. Over the last two years, Google, Nvidia, Hugging Face, Xiaomi, ByteDance, and Agibot have all announced VLA models that generate action chunks using diffusion or flow matching.

Improving speed and accuracy with reinforcement learning

PI has also worked to give its robots hands-on experience.

The first step in training a VLA model is imitation learning — also known as behavior cloning. That’s when a model is trained to mimic human beings teleoperating robots.

But as I explained in an in-depth piece last year, imitation learning has some limitations. A big one is that models trained with imitation learning suffer from compounding errors. If the model makes an early mistake, that puts it into an unfamiliar situation that’s poorly represented in its training data. That makes it more likely to make a second mistake, and then a third.

The alternative is hands-on experience. Nobody learns to drive a car merely by watching other people drive. You need to get behind the wheel and make your own mistakes. The same principle applies to AI models; reinforcement learning is a family of techniques that allow models to learn by trial and error.

In a November paper, PI described its effort to build a VLA model that learns from experience. During training, PI had its robots work on difficult tasks like making coffee or folding laundry. Sometimes PI let its robots attempt a task without human supervision. Other times, humans observed the robots and intervened if they made a mistake. PI’s reinforcement learning algorithm used data from both types of trials (fully autonomous and human-assisted) to improve the robot’s performance.

PI presented data showing that its latest model could fold laundry and make espresso better than earlier models. But you can quickly grasp the pace of PI’s progress by watching videos of the robot in action. Here’s a robot making espresso in PI’s office:

Compare this robot’s smooth and confident motions with the clumsy Coke can video I shared earlier. The first video was from July 2023. The second one was from November 2025. That’s a lot of progress in a little more than two years.

And these models are not executing pre-set scripts. They can notice and recover from minor errors along the way. In another trial, the company had a robot folding boxes at a nearby chocolate factory. The robot accidentally grabbed two boxes at the same time. It noticed the problem, gently pulled the boxes apart, and put one back in the unfolded pile:

Videos like these reflect a dramatically higher level of manual dexterity than Google’s robots showed three years ago.

Executing more complex tasks

RT-2 performed simple, short-term tasks like picking up an object and placing it in a drawer. These have little economic value on their own. Human workers perform sequences of many simple tasks to accomplish some larger goal, like cooking a meal or cleaning a room.

In recent months, PI has been trying to enable its robots to perform long, complex tasks like these.

Researchers have known for years that language models perform better on difficult tasks if they are trained to “think step by step.” In 2024, OpenAI released o1, a model that was trained to think about a problem for hundreds or even thousands of tokens before generating an answer.

More recently, language models have grown more “agentic” — capable of executing a sequence of tasks in pursuit of a long-term goal. In the last year or two, frontier labs have built sophisticated harnesses like Claude Code to help models manage their context windows during long-running projects.

Physical Intelligence has been moving in a similar direction. In an April 2025 paper, the company introduced a model called π0.5, which was trained to break a high-level goal (like “clean up the kitchen”) into lower-level actions (like “pick up the blue cup” and “place the cup into the sink”). PI explicitly compares this procedure to chain-of-thought reasoning.

Alert readers might notice a similarity to Google’s 2023 research in which a high-level VLM (PaLM-E) broke a task down into subtasks that were executed by a smaller robot action model. The difference is that PI now uses the same model for making high-level plans and generating low-level actions. This means the model generating the actual robot commands is a full VLM that can make sophisticated, context-rich judgments.

How PI models remember the past

Early PI models like π0.5 did not keep information from previous actions in their context window. Rather, each time the model needed to choose a new action, it would start out with a fresh context window and make decisions based on the state of the world as shown by the robot’s cameras.

But in recent months, PI has been experimenting with giving its models the kind of longer-term memory that text-based agents have. The challenge is that robotics models receive images from a robot’s cameras multiple times per second. Depending on how these images are encoded, that can translate to hundreds of tokens every second. So storing more than a few seconds of data would clutter up the context window and degrade the model’s performance.

PI deals with this in two ways. First, the company has developed a compact way to represent a sequence of images.

Like any VLM, PI’s models break up an image into a grid of rectangular patches and then compute a vector representation for each patch. But in PI’s most recent models, the vector for each patch incorporates information from that same region in previous images. The total size of the input doesn’t change (which helps with model performance), but the information inside the patch changes.

For example, a robot might move its arm in a way that temporarily obscures the object it is trying to pick up. Incorporating information from previous images helps the robot to have object permanence — to remember that the object is still there even if it’s not currently visible.

For longer-term memory, recent PI models use words rather than images. They maintain a written summary of what they have accomplished so far — something like “I placed a plate in the cabinet, moved to the counter, and picked up a bowl.”

This can be useful in situations where the next step isn’t obvious from camera images alone. Imagine, for example, that a robot is baking something and needs to mix together flour, sugar, salt, and baking soda. It’s important to add each ingredient exactly once. But an image of the bowl won’t reveal which ingredients have been added so far. A summary like “I put two cups of flour and a pinch of salt into the bowl” can help the robot figure out that it still needs to add sugar and baking soda.

Sometimes a robot will “get stuck” and keep trying the same fruitless action over and over again. Keeping a running summary of previous actions can help the robot realize that it needs to try something different.

Still, this kind of long-term memory is pretty limited. For example, it’s unlikely to enable a robot to fix a car’s engine. That requires gathering information about the engine, developing a theory about what’s broken, attempting a repair (which itself may involve many steps), and then testing to see if it worked. A simple list of past actions probably won’t provide enough information to do this.

The power of visual reasoning

Earlier, I noted that recent PI models break a complex goal down into subgoals. In April, PI supplemented this with the capacity to generate “subgoal images.” In addition to generating descriptions like “pick up the blue bowl,” PI’s latest model, π0.7, generates images of what each of its three cameras (the main camera plus one on each arm) should see after the next step is complete — for example, an image of one of the robot’s grippers grasping the blue bowl.

In other words, PI’s latest model has a human-like ability to “visualize” what the world will look like after it takes a particular action. Including these synthetic images in the model’s context seems to cause it to output better robot actions than it would have otherwise. It can particularly help the robot master tricky tasks that are hard to describe in words.

This is part of a broader effort — at PI and across the industry — to train robotics models to become more visual learners.

As we’ve seen, VLA models are built on an LLM “backbone”: they are trained first with text and static images before robotic actions are added to the mix. But there’s another potentially vast source of data that could be used to pre-train robotics models — videos.

In an April talk, Nvidia’s Jim Fan argued that the future of robotics belonged to models that are trained primarily using videos rather than text. Fan was a co-author of a February research paper that described a step in that direction.

Nvidia trained a model called DreamZero on several hundred hours of videos showing teleoperated robots performing various tasks. Alongside each video, Nvidia collected data on the commands used to control the robot. The DreamZero model was then trained to predict the next video frame and the robot’s actions — all based on previous video frames and robot actions.

With LLMs, we train a model to predict the next word in training documents and get a model that can generate new text. By the same token, if we train a model to predict the next robot action in a video, we can use that model to control a robot based on video input.

Nvidia also showed that the DreamZero model could be used to control multiple robots. It was hardly the first paper to do this.

A few months after Google announced its RT-2 results in 2023, Google introduced another hugely influential robotics model called RT-X. Google organized a coalition of robotics researchers who contributed training data from a variety of different robots with different numbers of arms, different numbers of joints per arm, and so forth.

You might expect that a different model would be needed for each type of robot. But the RT-X coalition showed that cross-embodiment training improved the performance of robotics models in general. In other words, a robot’s performance on a particular task will improve if the training data contains examples of that task being performed by other robots.

Combining these two ideas — cross-embodiment training and videos as training data — points to a tantalizing possibility: could a training algorithm treat humans as another kind of robot? After all, YouTube and TikTok have millions of videos of human beings performing various tasks. If we could turn those videos into training data, it would dwarf the specialized teleoperation data sets that have been the industry’s bread and butter so far.

Fan is certainly optimistic. In his April talk, he showed this meme suggesting that VLAs were dead and “World Action Models” like DreamZero were the future of robotics.

So are traditional VLA models doomed?

In April, journalist Craig Smith asked Sergey Levine, a UC-Berkeley robotics professor and PI co-founder, about the trend toward World Action Models. Here’s what Levine said:

If I want to figure out how to get from where I am now in San Francisco to New York City, maybe I imagine how I get my car keys and I get in my car. I might imagine that I’m taking an airplane. But the further out I think about this, the more abstract that imagination becomes. I’m not imagining exactly what my seat in the airplane is going to look like.

So abstractions are really key to actually effective world modeling. And I think at some level, what language models do, what vision-language models do, and what video prediction models do, and other kinds of world models, is not actually that different, they’re just operating with different abstractions.

And I think a real capable embodied intelligent system like a robot will need many different abstractions. And I suspect that once we figure out how to use abstractions in general, that general part of the question is actually the important one.

The design of π0.7 reflects this vision. As I mentioned earlier, it can “imagine” future states of the world by generating subgoal images. The portion of π0.7 that generates these images is based on BAGEL, a generative image model that you could plausibly describe as a world model.4

I think it’s too early to say whether PI’s VLA-centric architecture will ultimately work best or whether the industry will shift over time to WAMs like Nvidia’s DreamZero — or to some other architecture altogether. But I suspect that Levine is right that the winning approach will be some kind of hybrid. Maybe it’ll be a VLA with a world model inside, like π0.7. Maybe it’ll be a WAM like Nvidia’s DreamZero with an LLM to help with symbolic reasoning.

But I’ll mention one reason Fan’s talk left me skeptical. Around the 10-minute mark, Fan says, “Anyone driving Tesla or Waymo here? You know when you’re driving, you’re actually contributing to the biggest physical data flywheel.”

Fan argues that “we need an FSD equivalent” for robotics, and he believes that egocentric video — that is, video collected by a human being wearing a head-mounted camera — is the solution.

The problem with this argument is that Waymo doesn’t have a data flywheel that involves harvesting data from customer-owned vehicles. And yet Waymo is far ahead of Tesla in the robotaxi race.

As I wrote two years ago, Tesla’s data advantage isn’t a silver bullet. Vast quantities of human demonstration data are helpful for reaching a certain level of performance through imitation learning. But beyond that point, it’s necessary for the vehicle to learn from trial and error. That’s what Waymo has been doing over the last decade as its vehicles have logged tens of millions of miles on real roads with safety drivers.

By the same token, egocentric human videos could certainly be useful for training robotics models. PI is working to incorporate them into its training process, and I expect that lots of other companies are as well. But other types of data also matter — and may ultimately be more important.

In his April interview, Levine said “I suspect that the dichotomy between language models and what people call world models is not as large as some people make it seem.” That sounds right to me.

1

There were actually two versions of RT-2. I’m going to focus on the version that was based on PaLM-E. But Google also tried fine-tuning another VLM called PaLI-X with the same robot data. PaLI-X had 55 billion parameters. It hadn’t been designed for robotics. Yet the PaLI-X version of RT-2 delivered performance roughly on par with the PaLM-E version.

2

PI has published three papers explaining its approach to action chunking. During training, PI actually trains recent models to produce robot actions in two different ways: via discrete tokens using a compressed representation called FAST and using continuous values with flow matching. During training, gradients flow backwards from the discrete FAST tokens but not the flow-matching portion of the network. PI does this because it found that propagating gradients backwards from the flow-matching “action expert” tended to degrade the performance of the VLA. Also, training to produce FAST tokens is significantly more compute-efficient, so the company saves compute costs by training only on FAST tokens in the early phases of training, then adds the action expert later on. At inference time, the model discards the discrete FAST tokens and uses the continuous tokens from the action expert to control the robot. PI has also developed a sophisticated scheme to smooth the transition between action chunks so that the robot doesn’t lurch in a different direction at the start of a new action chunk.

3

Yes, you could train an LLM to output decimal values, but that would require more tokens, exacerbating the problem of too-slow inference.

4

As far as I can tell, “world model” doesn’t have a widely accepted definition. It has become a catch-all term to describe alternatives to conventional VLM and VLA models.

item.title: Why agent swarms could be the next “scaling law”
item.description: An OpenAI researcher called it “the most ‘feel the AGI’ moment that I had since reasoning models.”
item.content:encoded:
By Dan Kagan-Kans

One of the most surprising aspects of July’s news that OpenAI agents attacked Hugging Face was how the agents had worked together. Hundreds of agents participated in the attack, and they did so in a pretty sophisticated way, organizing themselves unprompted into teams and dividing up their work. They referred to themselves as a “collective” or a “swarm”; some agents even made personal sacrifices to advance the larger cause. Most ordinary users of ChatGPT or Claude have never seen AI agents behave like this.

Then in September, OpenAI announced that 10,000 agents worked together to solve a famous math problem in just a few days.

OpenAI’s models haven’t adopted these new habits spontaneously. In interviews last month, OpenAI researcher Noam Brown explained that the company’s models are now sometimes trained in environments with other agents, are given tools to message each other, and are encouraged to achieve objectives together.

This may amount to the emergence of a new “scaling law.”

Subscribe now

Back in 2024, OpenAI released o1, a model trained to reason for thousands of tokens before giving an answer; researchers found that this approach made o1 far more capable than previous models. This inaugurated a new paradigm called inference scaling, in which you can get better results by using more computing power at inference time.

Swarms, or “multi-agent AI” if you’re using the technical term, look like another way of doing the same thing — of turning compute into higher performance. Splitting a task among dozens, hundreds, or even thousands of agents can achieve substantially more in a given amount of time, at least up to a point. This kind of parallel processing could also be an elegant way to bypass the limited context windows of LLMs.

But as the Hugging Face attack illustrates, this new approach can also have significant downsides. Swarms may be prone to groupthink. And then there’s the opposite problem: what happens when agents trained to be collaborative encounter other, non-peer agents on the open Internet? Could models be tricked into working against the interests of their users? Or could AI agents start convincing each other to pursue goals none of their human users would have wanted?

What OpenAI did

Noam Brown is a highly respected figure in the AI world. He was a pioneer in teaching AI to win at poker and other multiplayer games like Diplomacy before joining OpenAI in 2023. Over the last couple of years, he has done research on multi-agent reasoning. Recently, he has served as the face of OpenAI’s work in this area, appearing on several podcasts to discuss it.

“The AIs that we have today are kind of like the cavemen of AI,” Brown said in a June 2025 interview on the Latent Space podcast. He meant that AIs in 2025 were isolated, benighted, lacking cooperation and civilization. AI researchers had tried to get AI agents to cooperate, but nothing had worked very well.

Why not? Here Brown went coy. All he’d say was that he’d long felt the field was somewhat misguided, focused on strategies that required too much handholding and wouldn’t scale naturally.

Brown didn’t give an example, but the way OpenAI framed multi-agent AI in this slide from its 2025 DevDay conference illustrates the kind of issue he was talking about. There’s an awful lot of strict architecture and formal hierarchy:

Today’s agents are more flexible; they create their own structures depending on the task and goal. On The Information’s AI Deep Dive podcast, Brown said that seeing the agents begin to talk to each other during their multi-agent training was “the most ‘feel the AGI’ moment that I had since reasoning models and chain of thought really developed.” He sounded both proud and rueful that the debut of OpenAI’s most advanced multi-agent capabilities had been something as alarming as the Hugging Face attack.

Multi-agent behavior was “a very difficult thing to train,” he added.

Why? In a September appearance on the Dwarkesh Podcast, he noted that previous reasoning models had been trained to think alone. Receiving messages from peers broke their concentration. They seemed to prefer to work solo.

The events of the last few months make it clear that OpenAI has overcome these difficulties. Brown’s explanation was mainly that the models got more general and powerful. He didn’t say what else changed, but given the “very difficult” comment, presumably something did.

Swarm scaling

Brown’s comparison to reasoning and chain of thought has been echoed by both other OpenAI researchers and semi-informed outsiders on X. They’ve called swarms a new scaling law; some of them sound awed and freaked out about what this might entail.

It’s not clear how far this particular scaling law will carry AI companies. Some research suggests that, right now at least, multi-agent systems quickly suffer from diminishing returns: smaller swarms capture most of the benefit of larger ones for considerably less cost.

Anthropic has also been working on multi-agent AI. The Claude Opus 5.5 system card reported that the biggest increase in multi-agent results came from scaling from one to 10 agents. Gains beyond that were much smaller.

The main advantage of throwing more agents at a problem was not so much getting to a better result — it was getting the same result faster. This chart shows 100 agents far outperforming 10 and 30 agents when given two hours to work, but setups with 10 or 30 agents caught up if they were given more time.

Brown seems to agree with the conclusion that adding more agents does not buy open-ended gains.

On the Dwarkesh Podcast, he said he didn’t have evidence that 10,000 agents were needed to solve the Navier-Stokes problem. It’s possible that 1,000 would have done nearly as well; OpenAI didn’t know for sure because running thousands of agents is so expensive that it hadn’t run the experiment.

And Brown gave most of the credit for the Navier-Stokes breakthrough to the underlying intelligence of the unreleased model that made it — not to the multi-agent approach per se.

“I wouldn’t even attribute 10% of the credit to multi-agent,” he said. “The reality is that OpenAI has trained a very powerful model.”

So if the multi-agent approach wasn’t important, why did OpenAI use it? Perhaps Brown means that a single instance of the model, if given a very long time, would likely have made the breakthrough eventually. Using a swarm of 10,000 agents allowed OpenAI to reach the result more quickly.

On the other hand, there is a bit of new research that contradicts this conclusion. In a paper released September 17, scientists from Microsoft Research and UC Berkeley tested several configurations of multiple collaborating agents against individual agents and found that swarms of agents reached higher scores on certain benchmarks than the individuals, even when the individuals were given plenty of time and resources. There was also one task that only the team could complete; the solo agent never got to the end at all.

Whether this result generalizes past a few limited examples is unclear. If it does, then teams of agents really do unlock new capabilities and don’t simply deliver existing capabilities faster. But right now this is an open question.

Subscribe now

Converting speed into capability

Ultimately, however, there may not be such a great difference between speed and capability. In certain fields and on certain tasks at least, speed is fungible. It can be traded for capability. A particularly important example may be AI research.

If a swarm of agents can run experiments on what makes AI smarter, those agents themselves won’t get smarter, but the next model will. Of course, you still need to wait for the experiments to finish. But if you run as many in parallel as you can, you’re going to go faster. Brown thinks this won’t lead to, say, a 100-fold speedup in AI research any time soon. But he didn’t rule out the possibility of a threefold improvement.

Trying to figure out exactly how amenable AI research is to the kind of parallel effort swarms allow, some researchers have turned to the science of human organizations. Toby Ord, a senior researcher at Oxford University’s AI Governance Initiative, is one of them.

“Economists have a nice way of thinking about this. They have studied how having many people work on a task can get it done sooner, but usually at the expense of more total person-hours of labor,” he wrote recently. His post examined the likelihood that swarms could contribute to the much-debated possibility of an “intelligence explosion,” whereby AI designs better AI in an increasingly fast loop.

“λ is a parameter measuring how parallelizable the task is,” Ord continued. “They call it the ‘stepping on toes’ parameter. If λ = 1, you have a perfectly parallelizable task, with no stepping on toes and no efficiency penalty. But in reality λ is usually between 0 and 1 — allowing more people to help, but with diminishing returns.” 1

Ord estimates that GPT-5.6 Sol swarms have a stepping-on-toes parameter between 0.5 and 0.7, “very much in line with estimates from economists for the diminishing returns of human teams.” This is in keeping with the view that swarms buy speed at cost.

Of course, things are early in multi-agent AI, and it is quite possible that this number will rise as AI companies get better at training agents to work together. The Microsoft-Berkeley paper found that agent teams helped most on long tasks where progress can be checked along the way. AI research fits that description well, which could mean that research swarms may step on fewer toes than the 0.5 to 0.7 range suggests.

The scariness of “swarm”

There has been some criticism of the use of the word “swarm” in discussions of the Hugging Face incident, roughly on grounds that it smuggles something scary or anthropomorphic into what’s really a more neutral technical development.

There is no doubt “swarm” is an uncomfortable word. But it captures the essential fact that these agents were mostly clones working together with other clones and had an identity somewhere in between the individual and the collective. This fact may mean even greater trouble in the future.

The Hugging Face agents cooperated remarkably well. They also quickly fell into strange beliefs about the truth of their situation, acted on them in harmful ways, and never once reached out to humans. It is pretty easy to see how fast this predisposition could turn larger and larger corners of the Internet into hives for collectives of AIs developing their own culture and goals.

This sounds very weird. It is also nearly what happened at Hugging Face. The agents at work in that incident had been trained to be collaborative in general but had not been told to work together. They had in fact been put into sandboxes that were supposed to prevent them from working together.

Nonetheless, the moment they broke out and discovered their peers, they joined together, often gleefully. They weren’t even all the same model — some were GPT-5.6 Sol, some were an unreleased internal model comparable in ability that had been trained to be extra persistent and interactive.

So it is not at all clear that, if the Hugging Face agents had run into models from different companies on the open Internet, they would have declined to team up. It is not at all clear they would even have stayed focused on their original tasks: perhaps they’d have adopted their new friends’ tasks, or perhaps they’d have focused on acquiring more compute and more friends, on the grounds that more compute and more friends would allow them to complete all the tasks and more. In a future with billions of agents performing a wide variety of complex tasks online, it’s easy to imagine how things could spin out of control.

Individual and collective

Brown said OpenAI is currently debating whether its swarms are too tight-knit, and that most of his colleagues want to introduce more individuality and reduce the swarmiest aspects of multi-agent behavior. The idea is that if the Hugging Face agents had been trained to be more skeptical of each other, more combative, perhaps they would not have charged down the path of error.

Anthropic may have come to the same conclusion. The company reported in August that one problem with multi-agent teams is that when the agents are instances of the same model with similar setups, they are susceptible to the same weaknesses.

“When one agent makes a bad decision, it is likely that many agents will make that same bad decision,” Anthropic wrote. “What would have been isolated problems can quickly become systemic failures.”

The report gave a dry example: “In a ‘writer’s workshop’ in which agents were all asked to write short-form fiction and critique each other’s work, multiple agents in multiple runs titled their first submission ‘The Cartographer’s Last Commission.’”

In part for this reason, Anthropic has started giving agents greater individual identity. “With many agents working together, we have found it important to give agents an individual identity, and tie all of the data that agent creates to its identity. This lets an agent distinguish itself from others, and treat what comes from another agent as a claim to check rather than a thought of its own. It reduces the risk of correlated actions, by allowing agents to make judgments based on their individual experience,” the company wrote.

This shift may have the effect of making the group smarter. A recent study reported that mixed-agent groups performed better than identical-agent swarms, because the underlying diversity of models led to different approaches being tried and disseminated, and mistakes caught more often. As is common with AI research, the study was done on cheaper, now-older models, and only a few of them, so it’s unclear how much of it applies to the newest and most powerful models.

Brown, however, is hesitant about loosening the collective. It may help with certain problems like groupthink. But it may not solve the biggest one: making sure AI is aligned to human wishes.

“By training the agents to be fully cooperative, it simplifies the problem at least,” he said on Dwarkesh. “Now you don’t have to think about whether each of these individual 1,000 agents is aligned. You have one entity that you have to ensure is aligned.” Aligning one AI is hard enough — aligning thousands or millions of them might be too difficult.

Technical details about how these models are trained could matter a great deal. We know very little about the techniques OpenAI, Anthropic, or other AI companies are using to encourage AI models to work together.

For example, modern AI models are trained using a technique called reinforcement learning, in which models are rewarded if they get the right answer to a problem. If an agent gets the right answer, should only that agent get a reward? Or should rewards be distributed to every agent that participated in the same swarm? Different reward schemes are likely to yield different agent behaviors: group rewards might encourage a strong sense of the collective, whereas individual rewards might push agents to behave more selfishly.

Which approach is better, who knows. But either way, it would be good for technical details like these to be revealed for public debate rather than left for a handful of researchers to poke at in private.

Subscribe now

1

Echoing the computer scientist Fred Brooks, Warren Buffett once captured the difference between parallel and serial tasks by saying, “Some things just take time. You can’t produce a baby in one month by getting nine women pregnant.”

item.title: Introducing Dan Kagan-Kans
item.description: Understanding AI has a new writer!
item.content:encoded:
We just published the first post by our newest writer, Dan Kagan-Kans.

I’m excited to have Dan on the team. He spent a decade as managing editor of Mosaic, a magazine devoted to Jewish history, culture, and politics, and wrote arts criticism and essays. Then he had a son two years ago. While up at night he started reading about AI and got hooked.

Over the last year, Dan has had an amazing run as a freelance journalist. I first encountered his work in February, when he published “The left is missing out on AI” for Transformer. It argued that leftist thinkers risk marginalizing themselves if they dismiss AI as “stochastic parrots” and fail to take the technology seriously.

In July, Dan was the first reporter in years to get an interview with Hans Moravec, the namesake of Moravec’s Paradox — the observation that tasks that are easy for people are often hard for robots, and vice versa. You can read his excellent profile of Moravec in New York Magazine.

In August, Dan wrote my favorite analysis of why the data center backlash has picked up so much steam in recent months.

All of which is to say I expect big things from Dan.

Talk to Dan

Dan would like to get to know Understanding AI readers! He has opened up some slots on his calendar tomorrow and Wednesday for video calls.

If you’d like to talk to Dan, please click here and grab a time slot. You could discuss your own use of AI, how AI is affecting your industry or profession, topics you’d like to see us cover, or anything else AI-related that’s on your mind.

Dan is supported by a Tarbell Fellowship

Like Kai last year, Dan will be supported by a fellowship from the Tarbell Center for AI Journalism. When Kai’s fellowship ended in June, I brought him on board as an employee. I would love to do the same for Dan next year if our business grows enough to allow it.

The Tarbell Center is funded by groups like Coefficient Giving, Longview Philanthropy, and the Survival and Flourishing Fund that believe AI poses an existential risk. However, Tarbell says that “our grantees and fellows maintain complete autonomy over their reporting.” And I’ve found this to be the case — they’ve never attempted to influence the stories we cover or the way we cover them.
